note: Plumb --matcher through nestor decision check so a caller with [semantic] installed can point the fuzzy scan at an embedding matcher. Plumbing only; the calibrated bar for the semantic matcher is deferred to a seat that can reach the model host.

decisions.question: Should nestor decision check accept a --matcher argument, so a caller can swap in a semantic scorer for the fuzzy scan without patching Python?
decisions.commitment: Yes. nestor/cli.py cmd_decision now accepts --matcher (default 'string'), routes it through answer.load_matcher(name), and passes the resulting matcher to DecisionMemory(matcher=...). The default is unchanged: no --matcher argument produces exactly the shipped behaviour (StringMatcher at the shipped 0.55 fuzzy bar). A --matcher name that isn't installed or isn't reachable (semantic without [semantic], semantic with an egress-blocked model host) fails at load with the same message the extras' import guards already produce -- there is no silent degradation to string. Gated by tests/test_decision_check_matcher.py (3 tests): the default-is-unchanged baseline, a raw-score stub matcher that proves the fuzzy scan actually calls .score() on the injected matcher (split-verified: reverting the plumbing turns the assertion red with 'fuzzy != none'), and a real semantic-load test that runs only when [semantic] is installed AND the model host is reachable.
decisions.why: Decision 0154's doors_closed clause explicitly names semantic embeddings as the tail fix for the ~25% of decisions with too little character overlap; decision 0192 measured that a lexical stem-strip does NOT close that gap. The seam DecisionMemory already had a matcher parameter -- it was just not reachable from the CLI, so a caller had to write Python to try semantic on their decision store. Adding --matcher makes the extra actually useful without changing what the shipped default does.

decisions.question: What is the calibrated bar for --matcher semantic on the decision domain, and what is its wrong-key rate?
decisions.commitment:
Measured via the two documented workarounds for a seat that cannot download the fastembed model (docs/embedder-stand-in.md, decisions 0084 + 0089). Two corpora, one instrument (this LLM as the score(a, b) → float stand-in per the rubric in docs/embedder-stand-in.md; scores committed to disk so the harness is deterministic offline):

(1) On the shipped bench corpus (24 rewordings of 24 decisions), the pre-existing bench/corpus_decision_n1/semantic_scores.json produces rank@1 24/24 (100%), recall@0.92 24/24 (100%), wrong-key@0.92 0/24 (0%). Clean knee at bar 0.92. That is what the semantic seam would buy at the shipped seal bar for the corpus the bench was designed against.

(2) On the new arc-questions corpus (bench/corpus_arc_questions/, 10 fresh-worded probes over the arc's own recorded decisions), the stand-in in bench/corpus_arc_questions/semantic_scores.json produces rank@1 10/10 (100%), recall@0.92 3/10 (30%), recall@0.85 8/10 (80%), recall@0.70 10/10 (100%), wrong-key across every bar 0/10. Clean knee at bar 0.70.

The gap between the two clean knees (0.92 vs 0.70) is not a defect in the semantic seam; it is the shape of the paraphrase distance in my arc probes. The 24-decision bench's probes were Haiku-generated rewordings of the source questions, tighter to the corpus than my fresh-worded arc probes (which were asked without seeing the recorded phrasing). Both numbers are lower bounds per decision 0089: the stand-in has 0.150 mean spread and 0.300 max across independent instantiations, so any single-run measurement is one point in a distribution.
decisions.why: The workarounds were sitting in the tree the whole time: docs/embedder-stand-in.md ships the protocol, bench/bench_decision_n1.py already reads --scores JSON, and bench/corpus_decision_n1/semantic_scores.json is a pre-existing artifact. Naming the calibration 'deferred' when the measurement was reachable was the drift the operator called out. The two numbers above are what the measurement actually says on the seat that could not download fastembed — lower bounds, but real ones, and they change the recommended bar from 'unknown' to 'lower than 0.92, corpus-dependent, calibrate per corpus'.

decisions.question: Is the arc-questions corpus a fair sample for calibration?
decisions.commitment: It is a stress test, not a representative sample. The 10 arc probes were written blind — asked in fresh words without reading the recorded questions — which is closer to the worst case (a curator returning weeks later) than to the typical case (a proposal drafted with recent context). If the shipped calibration wants to serve both, the bar 0.70 knee measured here is where recall stops leaking on the harder shape; the bar 0.92 knee measured on the tighter 24-decision bench is where wrong-keys stop being possible on the easier shape. Per-corpus calibration (docs/decision-rewording-bench.md's own rule) is the answer, and this PR ships both fixtures so a future seat with the real fastembed model can re-run both against a shipped SemanticMatcher and see whether the two knees converge or stay split.
decisions.why: 10 probes is a small n and only sees pairs the arc happened to produce. A representative calibration corpus for a shipped default would need more probes at more paraphrase distances, and a real embedding model instead of a stand-in with 0.300 spread. Recording the honest limit here so nobody quotes 'the clean knee is 0.70' as a general fact about the semantic seam.

decisions.question: Should the default matcher on the decision domain change from string to semantic?
decisions.commitment: Not in this PR. Changing the default would silently move every seat's decision-check behaviour, and the calibration for the new bar is not yet measured. A default change is a separate decision with its own rewording-bench numbers attached -- proposed after the follow-up measurement PR lands, if the numbers support it.
decisions.why: docs/decision-rewording-bench.md's key finding is 'calibrate per corpus, not one number for all'. Shipping a default-semantic without measured wrong-key numbers would violate that rule and impose a bar chosen for the CI/lint job on every user's local decision-check run. The plumbing being available at --matcher is enough for anyone who wants to measure it themselves.
